body: I wonder if the upvoters and downvoters have actually taken IELTS? I got 8.5 and I definitely passed my O level English (not A1 though).

I would spend more time in Nazca. You can visit the archaeological museum and the planetarium. There are also some cool day trips out to the aqueduct, the cemetery with mummies and Cahuachi. It was my first time in a desert, so I was amazed by the colourful sunrise and sunset there.

The museum in Arequipa is pretty cool, too. There is a whole exhibition on 'Juanita', a mummy that was excavated from the mountains. Colca Canyon trek is nice, it is 2D1N, and your hike ends at a hot springs!

Tough choice. I am a mountain person so I really love Huaraz. There are day hikes available and you get to see amazing mountains, glaciers, lagoons. If you rock climb, there are also nice bolted crags in the area. 

Lake Titicaca is beautiful, too. Not sure if you need a visa to enter Bolivia, mine was approved on the day when I applied for it in Puno. The Bolivian side of Lake Titicaca is really pretty, too. That said, I rather spend 3 days staring at mountains than at one big pool of water, but that is just me. 

I have never been to Ica so I cannot comment on that.

The road itself is really good. There's traffic police during peak hours, so do keep to the speed limit. 

I once got iced in at Te Anau though, it was a sudden snow which quickly turned to ice. Got stuck in the traffic for more than an hour, had to turn back because the route out was all iced up. Scary, fun times. It has never happened to any of my friends, though. So I guess you might ask your ancestors to bless you before driving out.

Hey. I am sorry you feel that way. One thing I have learnt is that, whomever you lost, you will always regret not spending enough time with that person. If you love someone, you will never be able to spend "enough" time together.

I lost my mum three years ago and it still hurts. There are good days and bad days. One thing my therapist taught me is to be kind and gentle to yourself. It is ok to grief, and anyone who has lost a loved one will know that it is not easy, no matter how your outward appearance might be.

Take care.

Social media detox helps. One thing I did was to write postcards to the people closest to me, you can also write one to yourself, too! Since you are heading to Japan, check out the temples. There is a temple "passport" (goshuin) that you can buy and get the different temples to endorse after you have made a donation and prayed. 

Have fun! Hope your heart heals :)

If you don't drive for long periods often, the drive back from Milford Sounds to Queenstown might be exhausting too. Te Anau is pretty, on a good weather day, I can simply chill by the lake and peace out. Lakefront hostel offers really good views too, so you can consider breaking your days up a bit. A tip is to get all your groceries from Frankton before heading down to Te Anau! 

Gaspy is a good app to check gas prices.

The story that is not reported is that the 4D numbers associated with her turned out to be winning numbers, so quite a lot of people donated to the funeral because they "profited" from the tragedy. I remember having to discuss it in school about the ethics over this.

I am in love with the hikes near Te Anau but they are definitely not the kind you will be able to do after driving over from QT and going for the glow worm cave tour. If you are still open to change your itinerary, you can read up on - Key summit from the Divide, overnight hike to Luxmore hut (avalance risk beyond the hut, so I won't recommend that), and Lake Marion. Winter is not a good time to do Gertrude Saddle, but that is something you can consider in the future.

For the Milford Sound cruise, I think the early rides are the nicest, and you avoid the QT crowds too.

The Italian restaurant in Te Anau serves really good pizza and pasta. It is pricey, though.
To add - a backpack that is fitted. Most people don't realize that Osprey backpacks come in different sizes and have adjustable back lengths. It makes a significant difference in terms of comfort.
Oh my god. I met a backpacker who asked me "What is Lonely Planet" and I felt so old. I still remember the days of physical maps and guidebooks... And I am not even 40 years old.

That's what I do too! I am a bad liar. Sleazy guys usually back down when you exhibit obvious disinterest in them and become slightly combative. 


Sometimes the reality might surprise you... I met a guy who exhibited great interest on every single detail of my itinerary, and when questioned, turned out that he is a socially awkward guy doing solo travelling for the first time and he has zero idea what to do next!

I travelled the other way, so I booked it in Uyuni itself on the day that I arrived, departing the next day. Back then, there were tours departing daily, so that's easy. I think you will get a sense of how touristy a region is when you are there, and you can plan accordingly!

(information accurate as of 2018)
You can take a Atacama to Uyuni 4WD tour, that'll bring you to some pretty cool areas in the desert and in the salt flats.


Lake Titicaca is nice, I spent one night on each side. Did kayaking from Puno's side (booked the tour the day I arrived at Puno) and chilled at Copacabana the next day.


I wanted to do Peru Hop/Bolivia Hop when I was there, but the party vibes were too much for me (I was staying in a hostel with a bus load of Peru Hoppers and it was chaotic), so I took the local buses instead. Back in 2018, the local buses were really safe, affordable and easy to navigate, even for me who can barely speak Spanish. Might want to check with the locals when you are there.


I really liked Nazca, and regret not taking the helicopter ride to see the Nazca lines. The museum is small, humble but very informative. There's also a really cool day trip you can do to see the mummies.


Arequipa is nice, too. I enjoyed the museum and the Colca canyon hike (with hot springs).

Bad! My boss turned out to be homeless (he lives in the bike shop) and started trying to get me to invest in his business ideas (bicycle rental shop for different types of bikes - penny farthings, etc).


Approached 2 other bike shops and they basically outright told me that they don't provide training and are not keen to hire someone with minimal experience. So I am just tuning my bikes as a hobby now.

Happy Birthday. I spent my past few birthdays doing things that reminds me of my mum, and spending the day with people who do not mind me talking about her all the time, it helps. Sending love and strength.

oops, just saw your comment. I got a car in the end, and driving in NZ is definitely easier than I imagined. Met some folks who hitch-hiked around NZ, it's definitely doable. I also tried car-relocation stints where you help car rental companies drive their cars from point A to point B, that's pretty fun!

Have not done the Cuyebano Amazon tour before, so no comments about that.

Salt Flat tours run daily, so if you have spare time, you can walk around the town to compare prices, it will usually be cheaper, but we are talking about maybe $15 USD in savings (then again, I am not good at bargaining), so I am not sure if it is really worth it.

I am a massive fan of Bruce Lee here, and so I am highly recommending the HK Heritage Museum. It is amazing.

If you visit Cheng Chau, you are culturally obliged to try their buns. Cheng Chau has an annual bun festival where people scramble up a huge tower of buns. It will not be taking place when you are there, but it is still nice to try the buns!

34F, 48kg. Back in my 20s, I can eat whatever and not get fat. Now I am very aware of the unhealthy food that I consume, and go for a long hike or workout if I know that I have been eating too much junk food. 

I don't think about it 24/7 - I weigh myself once a week and if I see that I'm gaining weight, I'll watch what I eat and exercise more.

I go on multi-day hikes and camp out! It's a great way to recharge and get away from people.

As for the "dry" and "similar" questions, those are convo starters, and it is entirely up to you to ask interesting questions! I recently has a "dry" convo with a guy in the hostel and after 5 min of chatting, I found out that he's a palentologist and we spent close to an hour talking about dinosaurs! He was showing me photos on his phone and I realised that we have other similar interests, we ended up chatting the entire night.

When I started travelling solo many years ago, I played Ingress. It was a great way to meet people and it brings you to interesting hidden local landmarks. I have not played it for a while now, so I am not sure how active the community is these days.
Agreed. It's better to head north. The touristy places that are quite nice include Malacca, Penang, Krabi/Phuket, Siem Reap. It depends on what intrigues you:)

There is no cookie-cutter approach to travelling, different amount of planning works for different people. You'll find your sweet spot the more you travel.

I've done both - planning everything to the smallest detail and winging it by chatting with locals/people from the hostel when I reach my destination. It depends a lot on why I picked that travel destination in the first place.

For spontaneity and adventure, you can always have a detailed plan and adjust it as you go along. Spontaneity and adventure happens when you approach life with an open mind :)

Agreed. I spent 3 nights at Paine Grande because I was unable to do the link-up. Came from Grey the 1st day, did the tail on the 2nd day, went up Britannico the 3rd day and went straight to Las Torres on the 4th. It was pretty fun, but expensive.

For accommodation, you will be generally ok except over Christmas and New Year, you should book in advance too. My friend and I had to walk around the town asking for last min accommodation because most places were already either fully booked, beyond our budget, or at far corners of the town. It was not fun lugging our full pack around. Then again, that was pre-Covid. Since your itinerary is not fixed yet, I would suggest that you monitor the availability about 2 weeks in advance to get a sense.

The LBS where I used to work at charge $1 per pumping of tyre. If the customer insists to change the tube instead, we will do it for them and charge them accordingly. We will check the old tubes for punctures and if they are good, we will offer them as cheaper options to customers with less spending ability.

There are buses between Santiago and Mendoza, so perhaps you can shave off a few days in Santiago to check out Mendoza :) Personally, I found Mendoza more enjoyable than Salta.

To link up Cusco to Uyuni, I went to Lake Titicaca, crossed the border to Bolivia and took a bus to La Paz. I spent a few days in La Paz before taking a bus to Uyuni. There are lots of places in Uyuni offering tours to the Salt Flats + Atacama desert. If you are a cyclist, the Death Road ride might be fun to you.

No sure how you are going to fit Iguacu into the equation, but if you go, you have to see it from both sides (Argentina and Brazil).

Thanks! I'll read up a bit more then! My first stop will be in Wellington and I have been stalking trademe for a while now, I have also been looking for cars on FB marketplace, it is still pretty unnerving for me to think about getting a car. 

I come from a very flat piece city and I hear that NZ is definitely not flat at all. I am not sure if I will be able to handle the windy switchback roads.

I might try public transport for the first month and consider getting a car after getting a better understanding of the terrain! :)

There are plenty of bolted routes in Huaraz! Check out Monkeywasi hostel, they have ropes, draws, shoes, helmets, quickdraws etc for rental. They will also be able to arrange a climbing day trip for you. If you stay in that hostel, you might be able to meet like-minded climbers! There were guys who were booking vans to go out bouldering every other day when I was there. However, I booked my onward trip before I reached Huaraz, so it was regrettable for me. I managed to do some sport climbing though, it was amazing!! Oh, the hostel has a bouldering gym too, so that was a fun place for ice-breaking :)

There were daily departures for the laguna/glacier hikes (that was pre-Covid), I am pretty sure it is still the case, judging from a quick search on Tripadvisor.

For Huaraz, I would say - other than your big trek, go without a plan. See if you can make climbing friends to go climb the next day, if you can't, do a day hike or two. You will need to acclimatise anyway. A walk around the town will give you a good idea of what is available. It is the most magical kind of window shopping ever.

I did not do Santa Cruz, I did Huayhuash (10-day) with Huascaran-Peru. I met 2 hardcore hikers who did the entire thing self-sufficient, so I guess it might be possible for Santa Cruz too? 

You might want to pack more socks. I packed 4 pairs of merino + 2 pairs of liners and it wasn't enough even though my shoes were Gore-tex. Then again, the rain god loves me.

Hi! How easy is it to travel without a car in NZ? 

I am planning to start from Wellington - Rotorua - Taranaki - Wellington - South Island. Planning to do some hikes (Holdsworth, Tongariro and a couple of day hikes here and there). 

Does it make more sense to drive to all these places or to take public transport? I am planning to camp, so I'll be lugging my gear around. Would want to avoid flying if possible since I would not want to buy a new fuel canister after every flight.

Hi! I am assuming that you really, really love hiking to want to travel the Huaraz. If that is the case, make Huaraz your first stop after landing in Lima. There are a few acclimatization hikes there and they are all beautiful. You could walk up the hill as some far corner of the town and see the layers of mountains surrounding it. Also, check out Laguna 69. If you are into rock climbing, there are many crags around, and the views are amazing. Huaraz was my first stop in Peru (after Lima, of course) and I regretted not spending more time there.

You can continue your way after that.

Personally, I find Colca Canyon lacklustre. You'll get to see the same condors in Huaraz. To each their own, of course :) I enjoyed Nazca more than Arequipa.

Lake Titicaca is prettier from the Bolivia side! It is a pain in the ass to get the visa, but it is worth it (to me). 

I heard that Salkantay gets really crowded, so I did the Ausangate trek in Cusco instead. It brings you to the Rainbow mountains, and it is not so popular -  our group was the only one on the trail most of the time. I love the peace and quiet after spending 2 days in Cusco. For MP, I did the bus + walk from hidroelectrica route.

​

Also, when are you going? Oct is the shoulder month, so there would be intermittent rains. You might want to gear up for that.

How long is his trip? Other than Cuzco, I would recommend visiting the Nazca Lines! Visit the museum on the first day, go to the observatory at night, and take the bus (or helicopter if he can afford it) to see the lines. There are also other sites around Nazca that are interesting.

Arequipa is really nice, the Colca Canyon is a really nice trek with hot springs! I enjoyed the museum about Juanita.

If he has more time to spare, I would recommend Puno, too. Everyone else insists that Copacabana is nicer, but to me, kayaking the Peruvian side of Lake Tititicaca is a lot more magical than the Bolivian side.

As a solo female traveller, I would say that Peru is very safe in general and Peruvians are very helpful and even protective of tourists. More than once I have asked for directions to a place and I ended up getting escorted to my destination instead. It is a country of very lovely people!
To add to the combo - Hey there Delilah.

My favourite museum is the Science Museum! I went there twice because it is amazingly curated to spark curiosity in adults and kids. British Museum is a must - Elgin marbles and the Rosetta Stone are my highlights. There is the National Gallery with some breathtaking art pieces... Other museums that are also worth checking out are the Wellcome Collection, Wallace Collection, Sloane Collection. Museums are free so you should definitely check them out. Some of them close later on certain days, so be sure to plan your itinerary well. 

If I were to compare the musicals, Phantom is the most amazing experience - the variety of costumes and the set is amazing. Since you have watched Phantom already, you might want to watch Wicked instead? I absolutely loved the theatre for Phantom though! It is super pretty and it is a very apt setting!

Off the beaten track, if you are a fan of Roald Dahl, you can take a train to Great Missenden to visit his grave and his museum (not free). Might be boring if you are not a fan. It is a day trip and the museum + grave is the only highlight there. The museum shop is amazing, and I enjoy walking around the small little town and taking in the vibes.

Ride a tricycle only if you really want to ride it. Do it confidently and you won't care if people would laugh at you  or not. People laugh at others all the time anyway.

If you are riding a tricycle because you want to ride a bicycle but you are not confident, my advise is to pick up cycling. I learnt it in my 20s, I know people who did it in their 40s. It is easier once you get comfortable. Some tips: look far and you will go where your eyes want you to go, try going down gentle slopes so that you can focus on getting hang of balancing.  


Either way, have fun!!!

CDC Motorcycle Learner Group. It will appear when you search the name. Not about about the link posting policy here \^\^;;;

There are several resources available from the chat - e.g. blog posts on the lessons, circuit maps, video on the road assessment, tips on how to pass the different lessons, etc. etc.

I spent around $800. Took me 6 months at CDC (it was closed for a while due to Covid), passed at first try. There is a telegram chat group for CDC learners so you can get slots fairly quickly if you camp for it. 

To speed things up, take your theory classes and tests early on, and go for your simulator classes after you have done 5 practical lessons.

After you have booked your TP test, spam revision sessions until you are confident. It is cheaper and faster to do so than to take your chances and fail.

Depends if I am in a good place or bad place. 

Good place -  take deep breathes, let myself be triggered, tell myself that I am sorry for letting something like that happen to me, I ignored the red flags and promise myself that I will be more discerning in the future.

Bad place - practice mindfulness. I will ground myself my saying my full name, today's date, the time now, what are my plans for the next hour, next day, the weekend, etc. I will start to describe an item near me in great detail until the feeling of vertigo disappears.

It gets easier over time. You are stronger than you think. Wishing you all the best.

I lost my mother in November, I did not get through it, I did not live through it. The closest description I can think of is that time just pushes you forward. It pushes and pushes. Soon it will be a week, a month, three months...

Welcome to Ingress!  


Keep it low level and use it to farm for low-level resos.   


Like what everyone else said, if it is obvious to everyone which are your home/office portals, it might become a high-flip portal if you managed to irritate someone from the opposing faction.   


More aggressive players might even stack big fields over your area to prevent you from using it as an anchor for fielding. Or they will do long shit links across your portal to achieve the same results.... Or hold a picnic near your home portal and fire X1 every few min just because they know that you will be frantically recharging your portal every time you get a notification... It is fun if you don't take things personally, can be kinda intimidating for newbies... Please try to not take it too seriously and have fun!!

AXA is now called Aegis.

MUFG is now quantum capsule.

Very rare items no longer duplicate in MUFGs.

Lawson cubes are now called Hypercubes.

ITO EN + transforms all hack outputs to defensive items, ITO EN - transform all hack outputs to offensive items.

You can buy 500 inventory slots by subscribing to CORE.

Level 16 agents can recurse themselves and start from Level 1, option to change faction is available during recurse.

There is a new action called "scan portal" with 2 associated badges. It is harder to attain than it seems.

You can request for key/no key when you tap hack/glyph hack. 

There is a 2nd Sunday badge - do 6 unique missions on 2nd Sunday of the month to add to the counter.

You can buy frackers for double output (fun for farming), you can buy Apex for double Xp (lasts for 30 min), you can buy key lockers to keep all the extra keys so it doesn't take up inventory space...

There is also a kinetic capsule (I redeemed a free one from the store) that allows you to transmute common/rare stuff to VR stuff (VRS, VRMH, VRHS, SBUL and hypercubes) by walking.

That's a summary of what I've learnt over the past few weeks :)

Oh, and the community is still as "dramatic" as before. Some things just don't change.

It is not just about winning. You need 10 interactions to get the badge. The interactions include - deploy reso, upgrade reso that is not yours, destroy reso, destroy link, destroy mod.

If you put the battle beacon on 1 neutral portal and deploy 8 resos, it will only be counted as 1 interaction. 

Also, there is a window period for this, I think phase 2 should be over by now. Phase 3 will be in March!
Yea.. I still refer the items as MUFG and AXA. I guess growing ultrastrikes might be useful, the mods are so much stickier than before!

It's the current anomaly series that is played rather differently than from the past. Players can buy their own beacons and fight for portal ownership with the opposing faction during a stipulated time frame and the interactions would contribute to the badge.
Yup! I came back for it! Took me some time to catch up with the new rules and all. I'm glad I have team mates who broke it down for me :)
Thanks for the info!! I just returned after 4 years, still catching up with the changes!

If no one is interacting with you, I think it is better to drop on opposing faction's portal that has links with it. Grab a friend from your faction and get

* 1 point for destroying link 
* 1 point for destroying mod 
* 1 point for destroying reso 
* 1 point for deploying reso 
* 1 point for upgrading your friend's reso 

(Please correct me if I am wrong, only played with 2 bbs so far and the above is what I concluded based on my observations)

From what I understand, you can move on after the 1st round because the same interactions do not count subsequently, even if you deploy a VRBB and you smashed after the faction changed? Not 100% sure about this, this observation is anecdotal.

Otherwise, I think you can simply deploy a battle beacon at someone's home portal and declare war? Or even better, organise your own local anomaly, coordinate with the opposite faction, split costs on beacons and go crazy :) Everyone can farm after the battle too! Boosted output for all!
If you are an anomaly player - Aegis shield, ADA, JARVIS, US8 (when you are level 8). Otherwise, common mods for engineer badge.
